name: Kingdom of Ireland
summary: The kingdom created when Henry VIII took the title King of Ireland (1542); ruled by the English, then British, crown through a Protestant elite while most Irish were Catholic, it was merged into the United Kingdom in 1801.

knownFor.label: Plantation of Ulster
knownFor.note: English and Scottish settlers given land.

location.value: The former Lordship of Ireland; after the Tudor and Ulster conquests the whole island was under central control from Dublin.

terrain.value: A low central plain of bogs, lakes and pasture drained by the River Shannon, ringed by coastal hills and mountains such as the Wicklow Mountains.

climate.value: Mild, wet oceanic climate warmed by the Atlantic, with cool summers, mild winters and frequent rain.

resources.value: Rich grassland for cattle and sheep, flax for linen in Ulster, timber (heavily cut in the 1600s), fish, and peat (turf) for fuel.

disasters.value: The Great Frost and famine of 1740–41, which may have killed over a tenth of the people; also harvest failures in the 1720s.

population.value: The page gives no population figures (the earlier figures of 2 million in 1700 and 5 million in 1800 are not stated there).

urbanisation.value: Dublin, the second city of the British Isles.

disease.value: Plague during the Cromwellian wars (1649–53), typhus (“famine fever”) and dysentery in the famine of 1740–41, and frequent smallpox.

migration.value: Settlers from Britain; emigration to America.

economicBase.value: Farming: cattle, butter and beef for export, grain and potatoes; linen weaving grew in Ulster from about 1700.

tradeRoutes.value: Salted beef, butter and hides shipped from Cork to Britain, Europe and the West Indies; linen exported from Belfast and Dublin to England.

wealth.value: Wealth was concentrated in a landlord class, many of them absentees living in England, while most tenants and labourers lived near subsistence.

moneyAndTax.value: The Irish pound, worth less than the English pound (13 Irish to 12 English from 1701); revenue came from customs, excise and the hearth tax.

governmentType.value: Established in 1542 by the Crown of Ireland Act, making Henry VIII king; a Parliament with a House of Lords and House of Commons whose powers Poynings’ Law (1494) greatly limited until it was repealed in 1782.

keyRulers.value: The kingdom was established in 1542 by the Parliament of Ireland through the Crown of Ireland Act; the executive was headed by the Lord Lieutenant. Poynings’ Law (1494) limited the Parliament until its repeal in 1782 gave legislative independence (“Grattan’s Parliament”). Cromwell is not mentioned in the part of the page read.

succession.value: The crown passed with the English (from 1707 British) crown, so the monarch of England was automatically King or Queen of Ireland.

institutions.value: Irish Parliament; Penal Laws against Catholics.

stability.value: Major uprisings in 1641 and 1798, plus the Nine Years’ War (1594–1603) and Williamite War (1689–91); the 1700s were calmer until the 1790s.

armyAndTech.value: A separate Irish military establishment of British regular troops in barracks across the country, plus Protestant Volunteer militias formed from 1778.

majorWars.value: The Nine Years’ War began in 1593 and ended with Tyrone’s submission in 1603; the Cromwellian conquest was followed by the Protectorate (1653–1659), though the page dates the conquest itself nowhere; the Williamite War (1689–1691) followed James II’s reign (1685–1689).

territoryChange.value: No change in borders: the kingdom always covered the whole island, though English control reached all of it only after 1603.

alliancesRivals.value: Bound to England; Catholic rebels sought help from Spain (Battle of Kinsale, 1601) and France (the French landing in Mayo, 1798).

inventions.value: Few inventions, but Irish-born Robert Boyle set out Boyle’s law (1662), and William Petty mapped Ireland in the Down Survey of the 1650s.

scienceEducation.value: Trinity College Dublin (founded 1592) and the Dublin Society (1731); Catholics were barred from most schooling by the Penal Laws, so “hedge schools” grew up.

openness.value: Open to trade, but English laws such as the Navigation Acts and the Woollen Act (1699) limited Irish exports until free trade was granted in 1779–80.

communicationTransport.value: Roads improved by turnpike trusts in the 1700s; the Grand Canal (begun 1756) and Royal Canal (begun 1790) ran west from Dublin; ships crossed to Holyhead and Chester.

religion.value: The substantial majority stayed Roman Catholic, while the Church of Ireland stayed the official state church until it was disestablished on 1 January 1871.

languageWriting.value: Irish was spoken by most people, especially in the west; English was the language of law, government and towns and spread steadily through the 1700s.

artsArchitecture.value: Georgian Dublin, including the Parliament House (begun 1729) and James Gandon’s Custom House (1781–91); writer Jonathan Swift and harper Turlough O’Carolan.

socialStructure.value: A Protestant Ascendancy of landowners at the top, then middlemen and large farmers, with Catholic tenant farmers, cottiers and labourers at the bottom.

sharedIdentity.value: Divided: Catholics saw themselves as Irish and Catholic, many Protestants as English in Ireland, and Ulster Presbyterians stood apart; by the 1780s some Protestants called themselves Irish patriots.

dailyLife.value: Most rural families lived in one-room cabins of mud or stone with thatched roofs, ate potatoes and milk, and paid rent in labour or cash.

neighbours.value: Great Britain across the Irish Sea (England, Wales and Scotland), with links to France and Spain through trade and Catholic exiles.

ideasReligions.value: The Society of United Irishmen (1791), inspired by the American and French revolutions, sought a republic uniting Catholics, Protestants and Dissenters.

colonisation.value: English conquest and plantations of settlers from Britain: Laois–Offaly (1550s), Munster (1580s) and Ulster (from 1609), then Cromwellian land seizures.

riseSignals.value: Lordship of Ireland founded in 1177 by Henry II, who had arrived in 1171; the Kingdom of Ireland was established by the Irish Parliament in 1542.

peakPeriod.value: Grattan’s Parliament: Poynings’ Law was repealed in 1782, granting legislative independence; the page gives no end date for the period.

declineSignals.value: The 1798 rebellion of the United Irishmen, crushed with heavy loss of life, convinced the British government to merge the two kingdoms.

outcome.value: The Act of Union of 31 December 1800 took effect on 1 January 1801, when the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland was created.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are well documented; population figures are estimates.
